blockMcqs.question: Why is access by index O(n) in a linked list?
options: The head pointer is recomputed each call
Nodes are scattered, so you walk from the head
Indexing locks the whole list
Each node stores its index, which must be scanned
blockMcqs.explanation: There's no address arithmetic; you follow k pointers one at a time.

blockMcqs.question: What distinguishes a circular linked list?
options: The last node points back to the head
Every node also stores a prev pointer
Nodes are stored contiguously in a ring
It can only hold a fixed number of nodes
blockMcqs.explanation: Looping the tail to the head means a naive traversal never terminates.

blockMcqs.question: Why does deleting a held node in O(1) require a doubly linked list?
options: Singly lists forbid deletion entirely
Doubly lists store nodes contiguously
You need prev to reach the predecessor cheaply
The next pointer is read-only in singly lists
blockMcqs.explanation: Without prev, a singly list must walk from the head to find the predecessor.

blockMcqs.question: Inserting after node p, what must happen first?
options: Set p.next = new
Set new.next = p.next
Delete p.next
Move the head pointer to new
blockMcqs.explanation: Overwriting p.next first would lose the rest of the list before you save it.

blockMcqs.question: What is the space complexity of Floyd's cycle detection?
options: O(n), it needs a hash set of seen nodes
O(log n) for the pointer stack
O(1), it uses only two pointers
O(n) to store the cycle length
blockMcqs.explanation: Tortoise and hare track position with two references and no extra storage.

blockMcqs.question: In iterative reversal, why save next before rewiring?
options: To keep the list sorted
Otherwise you orphan the rest of the list
It updates the tail pointer
To avoid a second pass
blockMcqs.explanation: Once curr.next flips to prev, the forward link is gone unless stashed first.

blockMcqs.question: What does a dummy node return at the end of an operation?
options: The dummy node itself
The tail of the list
A null reference
dummy.next, the new head
blockMcqs.explanation: The dummy is throwaway scaffolding; the real list begins at dummy.next.

blockMcqs.question: Why do arrays often beat linked lists despite O(1) inserts?
options: Arrays have lower Big-O for inserts
Cache locality makes contiguous reads far faster
Linked lists can't grow dynamically
Arrays never need resizing
blockMcqs.explanation: Scattered nodes cause cache misses near 100x slower than prefetched scans.
